description: We are a team of Computer Science students interested in building practical solutions with web technologies, data analysis, and machine learning. We focus on building practical, accessible solutions to real-world problems using technology.
summary:
We built CropPilot, a web app that helps Romanian farmers choose their next crops. The farmer picks a point on a map and enters their crop history, soil, irrigation, exclusions and priorities. The app then compares their current rotation with three alternative sequences of three crops each. Every plan shows sowing and harvest windows, scores for water, soil, climate risk and productivity, trade-offs, a confidence level, and checks to make with a local agronomist.

This answers the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA data into decisions about a specific field. We use 20 years of NASA POWER daily weather, along with SoilGrids soil data and SRTM terrain. Each rotation is replayed over the field’s real past seasons, so a plan that fails in drought years shows it. Survival Mode tests plans against the worst recorded droughts and heat waves, and a what-if slider shows how sensitive each plan is to warmer or drier conditions.

This matters because farmers often pick crops from habit while summers get hotter and dry spells get longer. CropPilot’s scoring is transparent and based on rules, with no hidden model. Missing data is shown as unknown rather than guessed. The app supports the farmer’s judgement and does not replace it.
details:
CropPilot is a web app that helps Romanian farmers plan their next crop rotation using NASA Earth data. Everything happens on one map page. The farmer picks a point on their field and enters the date the field is free, past crops, current rotation, soil if known, irrigation, crops to exclude, and their priorities. They can also add an optional what-if climate scenario.

The result has three alternative plans, each a sequence of three main crops, plus the farmer’s current rotation as a baseline. Each plan includes: sowing and harvest windows on a rotation calendar, scores for water, soil, climate risk and productivity, benefits, trade-offs and a confidence level, a rough money estimate, from county statistics, past prices and published costs (it never changes the ranking), things to check locally with an agronomist.

The engine works in three steps:

Field data: 20 years of NASA POWER daily weather, FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration, ISRIC SoilGrids soil properties and SRTM slope.

Evaluation: regional crop rules (calendars, successions, return intervals) remove rotations that don’t work. Each remaining rotation is then replayed over the field’s real past seasons.

Recommendation: the farmer’s priorities are applied, trade-offs are compared, and three clearly different plans are chosen and explained.

Benefits and intended impact

Many farmers pick crops from habit and last year’s prices, while summers get hotter and dry spells longer. CropPilot shows how each option would have performed on their own field in real drought and heat years. This helps them choose rotations that protect soil, save water and spread risk. The goal is to support the farmer’s and the agronomist’s judgement, not replace it.

How it is creative

Replay, not averages: each plan is tested season by season, so weaknesses in dry years are visible.

Survival Mode (“Challenge my plan”): every rotation is compared on the field’s worst recorded drought, heat and erratic-rain years.

What-if sliders for temperature and rain show how sensitive each plan is. They are clearly labelled as scenarios, not forecasts.

Plain-language explanations: an optional AI-written summary rewords the computed results but never chooses crops. A print sheet is ready for the agronomist.

Tools and technologies

Frontend and backend: Next.js (App Router), React, TypeScript and Leaflet maps.

Engine: Python with FastAPI, organised into data, evaluation and recommendation modules.

Shared contract: Zod, with generated JSON Schemas so the TypeScript and Python parts agree.

Optional public-data cache: PostgreSQL with Prisma.

Infrastructure: Docker Compose, NGINX on a VPS, GitHub Actions checks, pnpm and uv.

Data and references: NASA POWER, ISRIC SoilGrids, SRTM, FAO-56, FAO EcoCrop, FAO GAEZ v4 and Romanian crop technology guides (INCDA).

Hardware: none.

Factors we considered

Transparency: there is no dataset of “the right rotation”, so the decision comes from explainable, sourced rules and scores, not a black-box model.

Honesty about data: missing values are shown as unknown and lower the confidence. They are never filled with a default. Regional satellite data describes the area around the field, not the field itself.

Regional realism: sowing dates in the southern plains differ from Transylvania. The expert rules cover the southern plains, and other areas get lower confidence or an “insufficient data” answer instead of a guess.

Simplicity and privacy: no accounts and no saved farm data. One point on a map is enough, with no field boundary to draw.
